item.title: Navigation Assistant for Patients
item.description: Cancer patients in British Columbia face significant challenges in navigating care resources scattered across multiple providers and locations. Delays in accessing these resources can impact not only quality of life but even survival, for example when a patient cannot reach their cancer centre for chemotherapy or is unaware of a transportation assistance program. To address this gap, we have developed an AI-powered chatbot utilizing RAG technology, which generates reliable answers by drawing from a curated database of verified cancer care resources.

item.title: Fall 2026: Lab talks from Vancouver to Montreal
item.description:
It has been a busy fall for sharing the lab’s work.

  • ISBD 2026 (Vancouver, Sep 30): Dr. Nunez gave an oral presentation at the International Society for Bipolar Disorders Annual Conference on our chatbot that answers clinical questions using the CANMAT/ISBD bipolar disorder guidelines. The chatbot paper is now published in the Canadian Journal of Psychiatry.
  • Myeloma Canada Scientific Roundtable (Montreal, Nov 7): Dr. Nunez spoke on the opportunities and pitfalls of AI for better cancer care, drawing on lessons from our AI cancer care navigator.
  • Grand rounds: Dr. Nunez presented on what AI actually is and how we are using it in psychiatry at Sinai Health (Oct 9) and Royal Columbian Hospital (Oct 13). He also spoke on using AI to predict who needs psychosocial support at the Canadian Geriatric Oncology Conference (Oct 2).
  • Trainee presentations: Medical student Leah T’ien gave an oral presentation at the Canadian Academy of Consultation-Liaison Psychiatry Annual Meeting (Sep 24) on how AI should talk to patients with cancer about psychosocial needs. Medical student Danlin Zeng presented a poster at the 2026 ASCO Quality Care Symposium in Boston (Oct 16–17) on how social isolation relates to survival in cancer.

Congratulations to Leah and Danlin!

item.title: Three new papers from the lab
item.description:
Three papers led by the lab have recently been published or accepted:

  • A chatbot for the management of bipolar disorder (Canadian Journal of Psychiatry). We built a chatbot that uses an open-weight large language model to answer clinical questions, grounded in the CANMAT and ISBD 2018 bipolar disorder guidelines. Led by former undergraduate research assistant Yash Mali, with Jiao Zeng, Kayoung Heo, Grace Zhang and Antarip Kashyap.
  • Towards clinical implementation of AI in cancer care (Implementation Science Communications). A concept-mapping analysis of a province-wide workshop with patients, clinicians and leaders on what it will take to bring AI into cancer care in BC. Led by former MSc student Hong Hao Xu, with Chhavi Nayyar and Dan Hilbers.
  • Social isolation, psychological distress and survival in cancer (JCO Oncology Practice, accepted). A population-based study of how social isolation and psychological distress relate to overall survival in people with cancer. Led by medical student Danlin Zeng, with Jenny Zhang and Olivia Cook.

Congratulations to everyone involved!

item.title: New funding for the lab's AI work in cancer care and mental health
item.description:
We are grateful for several new awards this year that support the lab’s research:

  • Canadian Cancer Society Emerging Scholars Research Grant: Dr. Nunez received this grant to develop and evaluate our AI-powered cancer care navigation assistant, which helps patients find supportive care services at the right time.
  • UBC Faculty of Medicine New Faculty Research Award: supports work on evaluating the safety and reliability of AI-powered cancer care navigation systems.
  • IMH Marshall Fellowship: Clinical Research Fellow Dr. Kal Samarasinghe received a UBC Institute of Mental Health Marshall Fellowship, supervised by Dr. Nunez, to integrate structured reasoning into our chatbot for guideline-based treatment of mood disorders.
  • Mitacs Accelerate: Postdoctoral fellow Dr. Maryam Kamal joins the lab through a Mitacs Accelerate partnership with Sozo Intuition, developing an expert-level AI framework for real-time biotechnology intelligence.
  • Canadian Cancer Society Challenge Grant: Dr. Nunez is a co-investigator on Co.21-IMPACT, led by Dr. Kristin Campbell, which aims to implement physical activity programs for people with colorectal cancer.

Thank you to our funders and partners for supporting this work!

Dr. Nunez delivers keynote symposium at CAPO 2026 in St. John's, Newfoundland
item.description:
Dr. Nunez delivered a keynote symposium at the 41st Annual Canadian Association of Psychosocial Oncology (CAPO) Conference, held June 8–9, 2026 at the Sheraton Hotel Newfoundland in St. John’s, NL. This year’s conference theme was “A New Horizon: Expanding the Access and Impact of Psychosocial Oncology.”

The talk explored the potential benefits and risks of modern AI technology in psychosocial oncology, encouraging the audience to consider both the transformative opportunities and the important harms that need to be carefully managed as these tools are adopted in cancer care.

Dr. Nunez featured on CBC Radio's On the Coast: BC Physicians use AI Scribes to Document Patient Visits
item.description:
Dr. Nunez joined CBC Radio’s On the Coast host Gloria Macarenko to discuss the growing use of AI scribes in clinical settings, including the risks and benefits of using these tools to record and document patient visits.

You can listen to the full 7-minute segment on the CBC website.

This segment relates to our recent paper, Perspective: Listening to Users when Auditing Medical AI Scribes (Koenecke, Nunez, Rameau, Chen), which argues for more principled audits of medical AI scribes. While these tools offer real efficiency benefits, they pose risks through transcription errors and hallucinations that fall disproportionately on patients with speech disorders or psychiatric illnesses. We propose a framework involving diverse speech datasets, richer evaluation metrics beyond word error rates, and human-centered design research.

item.title: AI-Supported Physical Activity Behaviour Change for People with Colon Cancer
item.description:
Cooperating Researchers:

  • Dr. Kelcey Bland
  • Dr. Lauren Capozzi
  • Dr. Kristin Campbell
  • Kaela Cranston
  • Myles Chan

This project explores how an AI-powered chatbot can support people with colon cancer to become more physically active, building on the CHALLENGE trial (June 2025), which showed that structured exercise can improve survival. Because delivering individualized exercise counselling is resource-intensive, we are adapting an existing BC Cancer large language model chatbot to support exercise professionals to provide personalized, evidence-based behaviour change support.

Through co-design workshops with patients, clinicians, and exercise professionals, we will identify the features, safety needs, and delivery approaches required for a trustworthy and useful tool. A small pilot study will then assess the chatbot’s feasibility, usability, and acceptability. Findings will guide refinement and help determine whether the chatbot is ready for larger-scale evaluation.

item.title: Long-term tolerance to ADHD stimulants in youth
item.description:
Cooperating Researcher: John Ferreira

Credentials: MSc in Applied Neuroscience (student - co-supervised)

Interests: ADHD, Pharmacology

Education:

  • University of Western Ontario
  • University of Oxford
  • King’s College London

This project uses British Columbia’s province-wide PharmaNet prescription database (2005 to present) to study stimulant treatment for ADHD in children and adolescents. We retrospectively analyze three-year periods of continuous stimulant prescribing within each individual, looking for dosing patterns that may be consistent with pharmacological tolerance and how these patterns relate to age, sex, stimulant type, and cumulative exposure. Findings could inform safer, more effective long-term prescribing strategies for ADHD in young people.

item.title: Navigating Supportive Cancer Care: A Network-Based Analysis of Tumour Site Specific Pathways
item.description:
Developing network-based models to map how cancer patients access supportive care services across a complex healthcare system. Built dynamic visualization tools in Python to represent referral pathways and quantify transitions between providers. The project aims to uncover hidden patterns in care navigation, for example missed referral opportunities and delays in accessing mental health services, with the goal of informing system-level improvements in supportive care delivery.

Cooperating researcher:

Dr. Robert Grmek, MD (Resident Research Associate)

Dr. Robert Grmek, MD is currently a senior psychiatry resident at the University of British Columbia. His work focuses on the intersection of health care, technology, and health systems innovation. With a unique background in software development and medicine, he has developed clinical tools, including a psychiatric drug formulary app, and he has recently been focusing on using computational tools to better understand and optimize care systems as well as service delivery.

Interests:

  • Artificial intelligence
  • Digital innovation in healthcare delivery
  • Psychiatry

Education:

  • Bachelor in Computer Information Sciences, University of British Columbia Okanagan

Investigating fine-tuning versus zero-shot learning for general large language models when predicting cancer survival from initial oncology consultation documents
item.description: This study investigates whether fine-tuning open-weight large language models (LLMs) improves cancer survival prediction from oncology consultation notes compared to zero-shot approaches. Using Meta’s Llama models on 59,800 patient records from BC Cancer, fine-tuning consistently improved performance over zero-shot inference, but did not outperform smaller task-specific NLP models. The findings suggest both approaches merit continued investigation, with the best choice depending on clinical context and practical constraints such as hardware, privacy, and deployment feasibility.

item.title: Predicting Which Patients with Cancer Will See a Psychiatrist or Counsellor from Their Initial Oncology Consultation Document Using Natural Language Processing
item.description: This groundbreaking study demonstrates that artificial intelligence can predict psychosocial needs of cancer patients by analyzing initial oncology consultation documents. Different linguistic patterns predict psychiatrist versus counselor referrals, providing clinically relevant insights for patient care.

item.title: Machine Learning Prediction of Quality of Life Improvement During Antidepressant Treatment of Patients With Major Depressive Disorder: A STAR*D and CAN-BIND-1 Report
item.description: This study demonstrates that machine learning can predict quality of life improvements in depression treatment, supporting the use of early clinical indicators to identify patients likely to benefit from antidepressant therapy in terms of functional outcomes.

item.title: Response Trajectories during Escitalopram Treatment of Patients with Major Depressive Disorder
item.description: This study reveals distinct response trajectories to escitalopram treatment in depression by applying unsupervised machine learning to clinical data. The findings highlight that subjective mood and anhedonia are central to treatment response, while other symptom domains show more variable patterns.

item.title: Predicting the Survival of Patients With Cancer From Their Initial Oncology Consultation Document Using Natural Language Processing
item.description: This study demonstrates that natural language processing applied to initial oncology consultation documents can effectively predict patient survival outcomes across multiple cancer types. The models perform comparably with or better than previous prediction models while using readily available clinical data.

item.title: Using Neural Language Models to Predict the Psychosocial Needs of Cancer Patients
item.description: This doctoral dissertation explores the application of neural language models to predict and address psychosocial needs in cancer patients, contributing to the field of AI in oncology and mental health care.

item.title: Replication of Machine Learning Methods to Predict Treatment Outcome with Antidepressant Medications in Patients with Major Depressive Disorder from STAR*D and CAN-BIND-1
item.description: This replication and external validation study demonstrates that machine learning methods can successfully predict antidepressant treatment outcomes, with prediction of remission performing better than prediction of response. These findings support the clinical utility of machine learning approaches for personalized depression treatment planning.
